text.p: Germany's largest department store group Karstadt AG on Thursday announced a slowdown in business during the first three months of 1997, but said it was still on target to improve earnings this year.
Karstadt group sales fell 2.3 percent in the first quarter to 5.979 billion marks, and in the first five months both its Karstadt and Hertie chains lost trade on a same-store basis.

Chief executive Walter Deuss told the company's annual results news conference the group expected a "significant improvement" in earnings as long as forecasts of a mild recovery in consumer demand are realised.
In 1996, Karstadt's group net profits fell 46 percent to 58.6 million marks. Group sales fell slightly to 26.9 billion marks from 26.98 billion marks.
But costs of store closures at the loss-making Hertie chain left it with a per-share loss of 20.92 marks, little changed from its DVFA result in 1995.

Hertie had a 102.2 million mark net loss last year. Due to store closing costs, the bottom-line deficit was 241.4 million marks. But Deuss said Hertie was now fully integrated in group logistics operations and should be near break even this year.
Karstadt shares fell 27 marks in floor trading to 625 marks. Analysts said the main reason for the fall was news the WCM group no longer wanted to buy 25 percent of Karstadt.

Thursday's Handelsblatt business daily quoted WCM's main shareholder Karl Ehlerding saying he had abandoned interest in buying into Karstadt after finding prices sought by Deutsche Bank and Commerzbank for their 10 percent stakes too high.
"The WCM news was more important today than the new numbers," said analyst Max Resch of Vereinsbank Research.
Karstadt management announced a two-pronged approach to help turn around the group's fortunes.
The so-called "Busy" programme to improve efficiency and tighten up product ranges should cut annual costs by 250 million marks by 1999, board member Klaus Eierhoff said.
No savings will be achieved this year, but cuts should total around 150 million marks in 1998, he said.

Deuss said Karstadt would also follow up on the successful pilot project at its Duisburg branch, which it has refurbished to offer a "theme" approach to replace the old-style department store format increasingly shunned by German consumers.
The Duisburg store upgrade cost around 600 marks per square metre, but costs could fall at other locations, Duess said.
In addition, Karstadt will close a further 11 Hertie stores this year -- fewer than earlier announced -- and transfer a further two into the Karstadt chain.
Analysts welcomed the initiatives but said Karstadt still lagged behind rival Metro group's Kaufhof chain, which is ahead with its "Galeria" mall concept.

"The efforts should be welcomed, but it is not enough to make a big story out of them," said Joerg Christians at Trinkaus Capital Management. Both Christians and Vereinsbank's Resch kept their rating of Karstadt shares unchanged at "sell".

Deuss, in the job since 1979, has faced media speculation that shareholders might demand a management change. He declined to comment, but analysts said he would remain under pressure after Karstadt cut its 1996 dividend to 10 marks from 13.
The analysts also doubted whether he would be able to meet his target of this year trebling the pre-tax return on sales from last year's slim 0.24 percent.
